lessons.title: The team leader's role in poultry production
lessons.html:
The team leader's role in poultry production

On a poultry farm, small mistakes can have big consequences: a missed water check, an open door, or a skipped foot bath can cost thousands of birds. The team leader makes sure that routines are done correctly every day, by every worker, in every house.

Main responsibilities

  • Plan the daily and weekly work for the team: house checks, feeding, egg collection, cleaning, dead bird removal, catching or placement days.
  • Allocate workers to houses and tasks.
  • Brief the team at the start of the shift.
  • Check that work is done to standard and on time.
  • Make sure biosecurity and safety rules are followed.
  • Keep daily records and pass information to the supervisor or manager.
  • Report problems with birds, equipment and people immediately.

Routines matter

Birds do best with a consistent routine: same feeding, lighting and checking times every day. Workers who are well trained in the routine notice when something changes - lower water use, quiet birds, a strange smell. Encourage your team to report anything unusual.

Leading by example

If the team leader skips the shower or the foot bath, the team will too. Always follow the biosecurity rules yourself, wear PPE and handle birds gently.

Working with others

Team leaders work with the farm manager, the vet, maintenance staff, feed delivery drivers, catching crews and hatchery staff. Make sure outsiders follow biosecurity rules and that your team knows who is allowed into which houses.

Fairness

Treat all team members with respect and the same rules. Allocate unpleasant jobs, such as cleaning out or dead bird disposal, fairly by rotation.

lessons.title: Communicating and allocating work
lessons.html:
Communicating and allocating work

The shift briefing

Hold a short briefing at the start of each shift. Cover:

  1. Which houses each worker is responsible for.
  2. Special tasks for the day: vaccination, weighing, raising feeders, cleaning out, catching.
  3. Problems from yesterday and how they were solved.
  4. Safety and biosecurity reminders for today's tasks.
  5. Questions from the team.

Clear instructions

Say what, where, when, how and who: 'Thabo, raise the drinker lines in house 3 to the birds' back height by ten o'clock, then check every nipple line is flowing.' Ask the worker to repeat it back. Show new workers how to do it.

Allocating work

  • Give each worker clear responsibility for specific houses, so they know their birds well.
  • Use experienced workers for critical tasks such as vaccination and brooding.
  • Pair new workers with experienced ones.
  • Follow biosecurity in allocations: a worker should not go from older or sick flocks to young chicks on the same day if farm rules forbid it.
  • Plan cover for absent workers.

Listening and feedback

Listen when workers report problems; they are your early warning system. Thank them, act, and tell them what happened. Give praise for good work and correct mistakes privately and calmly.

Written communication

Use the house record cards, daily report sheets or app to pass information between shifts and to the manager. Write clearly: date, house, numbers, what happened, what was done.

Solving disagreements

Deal with conflicts early. Listen to both sides privately, focus on the facts and the work, and agree on a solution. Refer serious matters to the manager.

lessons.title: Safety, training and team performance
lessons.html:
Safety, training and team performance

Keeping the team safe

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, everyone must work safely and report hazards. As team leader:

  • Check that masks, gloves, goggles and boots are worn for dusty work, cleaning and chemical use.
  • Make sure fan guards and electrical covers are in place.
  • Stop unsafe work, such as climbing on feeders or using damaged ladders.
  • Make sure heavy feed bags and egg trays are lifted correctly or with help.
  • Know the emergency plan for fire, power failure and injuries.
  • Report every injury and near miss.

Power failure

A power failure in a closed house can kill birds within a short time from heat and lack of air. Make sure the team knows how the generator and alarm work, who to call, and what to do while power is restored, such as opening emergency curtains or doors if the farm's procedure says so.

Training the team

Train each worker in the routines of their house: checking birds, feed and water, ventilation settings, recording, dead bird removal and biosecurity. Use explain, demonstrate, practise and check. Keep a record of who is trained in what.

Measuring performance

MeasureWhat it shows
Mortality per houseBird care and health
Average weight vs targetFeeding, brooding, health
Egg collection and floor eggsCare in layer houses
Record completenessAttention to detail
Biosecurity checks passedRule following
Attendance and safety incidentsTeam reliability and safety

Share results with the team and recognise good performance.

Key points

  • Team leaders make sure routines are done correctly every day.
  • Brief the team each shift and give clear instructions.
  • Allocate houses so workers know their birds well.
  • Follow biosecurity yourself and in work allocation.
  • Prepare the team for power failures and report every injury.
